claims.text: The homogenized, annealed HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Heating HfNbTaTiZr through approximately 673–1073 K produces a plateau in its temperature-dependent stress–strain or yield-strength behavior.
The elevated-temperature plateau is caused by a transition from screw-dislocation-controlled deformation to edge-dislocation-dominated slip.
Atomic-size mismatch creates intrinsic lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Intrinsic lattice distortions promote the transition from screw-dislocation motion to edge-dislocation-dominated slip.
Screw-dislocation motion controls deformation at room or lower temperatures.
Increasing temperature thermally activates dislocations and enables them to overcome motion barriers more readily.
Lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr modifies dislocation core structures.
Edge-dislocation-controlled deformation is less temperature sensitive than screw-dislocation-controlled deformation.
A change to edge-dislocation control suppresses ordinary temperature-induced softening and produces a yield-strength plateau.
Relative to room temperature, HfNbTaTiZr exhibits only minimal yield-strength changes over approximately 673–1073 K.
Relative to room temperature, HfNbTaTiZr exhibits only minimal changes in elastic modulus over approximately 673–1073 K.
HfNbTaTiZr exhibits a moderated, nonlinear thermal-expansion response over approximately 673–1073 K.
Room-temperature HfNbTaTiZr behavior is characterized by continuous softening.
The HfNbTaTiZr microstructure remains single-phase BCC throughout testing from approximately 673 K to 1073 K.
The proposed behavior applies only before phase transformation or extensive dynamic recovery begins.
Concurrent dynamic recovery may affect the proposed dislocation transition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis sometimes describes a plateau in the stress–strain curve itself, but elsewhere operationalizes the prediction as a plateau in yield strength versus temperature. These are distinct measurable phenomena.
